To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
physicists want to be remembered by colleagues as having been a good person and a good physicist, and they want their work to be remembered as having been important.

the most highly productive and successful physicists in the most highly ranked departments wish to be remembered for their professional attributes, whereas the less productive and less successful physicists in the less highly ranked departments wish for their personal attributes.
physicists wish to be: remembered for professional contributions, remembered by colleagues who are themselves productive, and remembered as a good person.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how academics construct their legacy in the context of a profession where status is relational and reputation is a social fact.
the question of the social significance and social value of colleagues in academia.
how the social significance of others is used to create the social significance of the self.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social codes of honor and morality are not contradictory but complementary, and that they are used to project a legacy in a manner that is socially and institutionally strategic.
the academic profession is a status system, but that the status of colleagues is not valued by academics in the ways that one might expect.
the social significance of honor in the academic profession is not to be underestimated, and that it is a complex, multilayered phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
physicists are not as collegially minded as they might like to believe.
, while physicists are highly aware of the significance of colleagues in their work, they are also deeply ambivalent about the social value of their colleagues.
, in the case of physics, the desire of physicists to be remembered by colleagues reflects the social structure of the discipline.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in academia, honor is a social relation.
status is a social process in which people actively participate.
the professional and the personal are not mutually exclusive.
